THE STRATEGIC PARADIGM
BY COLONEL ADRIAN PARSONS (RET.)

There was a general in our forces, and he was wondrous wise;
He charged into a minefield and lost both of his eyes.
And when he saw what he had done, with all his might and main
He charged into another field and got them back again.
MILITARY FOLK SAYING

Colonel Stephen Porter found Captain Benjamin Anderson and the lieutenant waiting in his office when he arrived at the Queenstown Strategic Command Center that morning. Anderson looked as though he'd been up all night reviewing intelligence reports. There were dark circles under his eyes; his usually crisp uniform seemed rumpled at every seam. Porter glanced sharply at his Intelligence Director and sank down behind his desk with a sigh. "All right, Ben—what's wrong?"

"This lieutenant is driving me crazy," said Anderson through clenched teeth. "He's gone completely off the reservation. Nobody's been able to work with him for three weeks, and now at six o'clock this morning he decides he's resigning his commission. I talk to him, I reason with him, I do everything but lock him in the barracks, and I waste my time. He's resigning. Period."

"So you bring him down here," said Porter sourly. "The worst place he could be, if something's really wrong." He looked across at the young officer. "Lieutenant Russell? Come over and sit down."

There was nothing singular about the lieutenant's appearance. He was thin, with a pale face and the earnest expression of any normal twenty-five-year-old officer as he blinked across the desk at Porter. The standard tactical headset rested on the desk beside him. He sat with a mute appeal in his dark eyes as Porter flipped the analysis-switch and blinked in alarm at the wildly fluctuating pattern on the screen.

The lieutenant was in crisis. He was literally pulsating with professional doubt.

Porter sat back slowly. "Tell me about it, Matthew," he said gently.

"I don't want to go back to Crestwood Base," said the lieutenant.

"Why?"

"I just don't. I can't function there."

"Are you frightened?"

The lieutenant bit his lip and nodded slowly.

"Of me? Of Captain Anderson?"

"No. Oh, no!"

"Then what?"

Again the mute appeal in the lieutenant's eyes. He groped for words, and none came. Finally he said, "If I could only take this off—" He touched the tactical headset.

"You think that would make you feel better?"

"It would, I know it would."

Porter shook his head. "I don't think so, Matthew. You know what the headset is for, don't you?"

"It filters incoming strategic data."

"That's right. And it filters your analytical outputs. It's a regulator. You need it badly. It would hurt you a great deal if you operated without it, away from the controlled environment."

The lieutenant fought back his frustration. "But I don't want to go back there—" The crisis-pattern was alive again on the screen. "I don't feel effective there. I never want to go back."

"Well, we'll see. You can stay here for a while." Porter nodded at Anderson and stepped into an adjoining room with him. "You say this has been going on for three weeks?"

"I'm afraid so. We thought it was just a temporary pattern—we see so much of that at Crestwood. Usually officers work through these phases on their own. The structured environment there, the regular duties and training exercises—they provide stability. Most recover within days."

"But not Matthew."

"No. His case is different. The question is what to do with him now."

Porter chewed his lip. "I don't like it. We'd better set up a full evaluation on him and try to spot the trouble. And I'm afraid you'll have to handle the arrangements. I've got that young Dr. Parsons from Horizonville to deal with this morning—the one who's threatening to upset the whole Strategic Conference next month with some radical theories he's been developing. I'll probably have to take him out to Crestwood to address his concerns." Porter ran a hand through sparse grey hair. "As for Matthew—he needs to be kept separate from normal operations. No contact with senior staff. No participation in standard training rotations. Nothing that would expose him to command hierarchy."

Anderson frowned. "Complete removal from the regular schedule?"

"Complete removal from everything, Ben. Set it up downstairs. Total restriction—no briefings, no tactical exercises, no group work. Just evaluation protocols in a controlled space." Porter's voice hardened. "And in this case, be absolutely certain of it. If Matthew's in the trouble I think he's in, we don't dare risk unfiltered command exposure now. Keep all senior personnel away from him. We could end up with a broken officer on our hands."

Anderson nodded slowly. "I'll arrange for a private evaluation room. Restricted access. Only the monitoring equipment and essential staff."

"Good. Now I need to prepare for our visitor."

Two letters were waiting on Porter's desk that morning. The first was from Strategic Publications, announcing another shift of deadline on the monograph, and demanding the final proofs two weeks earlier than scheduled. Porter groaned. As director of strategic doctrine at the Queenstown Command Center, he had long since learned how administrative detail could consume operational hours. He knew that his real work was at Crestwood—yet he hadn't even been to Crestwood in over six weeks. And now, as the monograph approached publication date, Porter wondered if he would ever really get back to work again.

The other letter cheered him a bit more. It bore the letterhead of the International Strategic Doctrine Conference:

Dear Colonel Porter:

In recognition of your position as an authority on military decision-making patterns under stress conditions, we would be gratified to schedule you as principle speaker at the Conference in Horizonville on October 12th. A few remarks in discussion of your forthcoming monograph would be entirely in order—

They were waiting for it, then! He ran the final proofs into the scanner excitedly. They knew he had something revolutionary to propose. His earlier papers had only hinted at the direction he was going—but the monograph would clear away the confusion. He scanned the title page proudly. "A Theory of Command Influence on Junior Officer Development and Decision-Making Capacity." A good title—concise, commanding, yet modest. They would read it, all right. And they would find it a light shining brightly in the darkness, a guide to the commanders who were floundering in the jungle of a strange and baffling new doctrine.

For they were floundering. When modern warfare finally forced them to recognize that traditional hierarchical command structures were failing in complex operational environments, they had plunged eagerly into reform, and found themselves in a maddening bramble bush of contradictions and chaos. Nothing worked, and everything worked too well. They were trying to study phenomena which made no sense, observing things that defied classical military theory. Established doctrines came crashing down about their ears as they stood sadly by and watched outcomes that traditional doctrine said could never happen. They had never been in this terrain before, nor in any terrain remotely like it. The old rules didn't work here, the old methods of command failed. And the more they struggled, the thicker and more impenetrable the bramble bush became—

But now Stephen Porter had discovered a pathway through that jungle, a theory to work by—

At his elbow the intercom buzzed. "A gentleman to see you," the aide said. "A Dr. Adrian Parsons. He's very impatient, sir."

He shut off the scanner and said, "Send him in, please."

Dr. Adrian Parsons was tall and thin, with jet black hair and dark mocking eyes. He wore a threadbare academic jacket and carried himself with casual arrogance. He offered Porter a bony hand, then flung himself into a chair as he stared about the office with barely concealed contempt.

"I'm really overwhelmed," he said after a moment. "Within the stronghold of strategic doctrine at last. And face to face with the Master in the trembling flesh!"

Porter frowned. "Dr. Parsons, I don't quite understand—"

"Oh, it's just that I'm impressed," the young man said airily. "Of course, I've seen old dried-up Authorities before—but never before a brand spanking new one, just fresh out of the academy, so to speak!" He touched his forehead in a gesture of mock reverence. "I bow before the Oracle. Speak, oh Colonel, live forever! Cast a pearl at my feet!"

"If you've come here to be insulting," Porter said coldly, "you're just wasting time." He reached for the intercom switch.

"I think you'd better wait before you do that," Parsons said sharply, "because I'm planning to take you apart at the Conference next month unless I like everything I see and hear down here today. And if you don't think I can do it, you're in for quite a shock."

Porter sat back slowly. "Tell me—just what, exactly, do you want?"

"I want to hear this fairy tale you're about to publish in the name of 'Theory'," Parsons said. "I want to see this famous Crestwood facility of yours and see for myself how much pressure these experimental controls you keep talking about will actually bear. But mostly, I want to see just what in strategic hell you're so busy making yourself an Authority about." There was no laughter in the man's sharp brown eyes.

"You couldn't touch me with a ten foot pole at this conference," snapped Porter.

The other man grinned. "Try me! We shook you up a little bit last year, but you didn't seem to get the idea."

"Last year was different." Porter scowled. "As for our 'fairy tale', we happen to have a staggering body of evidence that says that it's true."

"If the papers you've already published are a preview, we think it's false as hell."

"And our controls are above suspicion."

"So far, we haven't found any way to set up logical controls in this field," said Parsons. "We've done a lot of work on it, too."

"Oh, yes—I've heard about your work. Not bad, really. A little misdirected, is all."

"According to your Theory, that is."

"Wildly unorthodox approach to strategic doctrine—but at least you're energetic enough."

"We haven't been energetic enough to find an orthodox approach that got us anywhere. We doubt if you have, either. But maybe we're all wrong." Parsons grinned unpleasantly. "We're not unreasonable, Colonel. We just ask to be shown. If you dare, that is."

Porter slammed his fist down on the desk angrily. "Have you got the day to take a trip?"

"I've got 'til New Year."

Porter shouted for his aide. "Get Anderson up here. We're going to Crestwood this afternoon."

The aide nodded, then hesitated. "But what about your lunch meeting with the General Staff?"

"Cancel it." He gave Parsons a sidelong glare. "We've got a guest here who's got a lot of words he's going to eat for us...."

Before they left, Porter checked with Anderson about the arrangements for Lieutenant Russell.

"Everything's set up," Anderson reported. "Evaluation room on the lower level. Sealed environment."

"And you've restricted all contact?"

"No one goes in except essential monitoring personnel. He's separated from all regular activities." Anderson paused. "Colonel, some of the staff questioned the approach. They pointed out that Crestwood's normal therapeutic environment has helped dozens of officers recover from similar crises. The regular schedule there—training exercises, collaborative work, structured duties—these things give troubled officers a sense of purpose. Several staff members suggested that returning Matthew to that routine might actually help stabilize him."

Porter shook his head firmly. "Not this case. The normal approach won't work here. Matthew needs complete separation—no duties, no exercises, no exposure to command structure at all. That's what I've ordered, and that's what we'll do."

"Understood. The restricted evaluation is in place."

Ten minutes later they boarded the military transport helicopter on the roof of the Queenstown Command Center. They sat in silence as the aircraft lifted off and headed northeast, skimming over the countryside toward Crestwood. The landscape below shifted from urban sprawl to rolling hills dotted with military installations. In less than forty minutes the helicopter was descending toward a sprawling complex of low buildings surrounded by high security fences.

"What's the status on Russell?" Porter asked Anderson as the helicopter settled onto the landing pad.

"He's secure in the evaluation room. Complete restriction from all regular operations."

Porter ground his teeth. "I should be monitoring his evaluation now instead of beating the bushes with this—" He broke off to glare at young Parsons.

Parsons grinned. "I've heard you have quite a facility up here."

"It's—unconventional, at any rate," Porter snapped.

"Well, that depends on your standards. Sounds like a military academy, from what I've heard. According to your papers, you've even used conventional statistical analysis on your data from up here."

"Until we had to throw it out. We discovered that what we were trying to measure didn't make sense in a statistical analysis."

"Of course, you're sure you were measuring something."

"Oh, yes. We certainly were."

"Yet you said that you didn't know what."

"That's right," said Porter. "We don't."

"And you don't know why your instruments measure whatever they're measuring." Parsons's face was thoughtful. "In fact, you can't really be certain that your instruments are measuring the officers at all. It's not inconceivable that the officers might be affecting the instruments, eh?"

Porter blinked. "It's conceivable."

"Mmmm," said Parsons. "Sounds like a real firm foundation to build a theory on."

"Why not?" Porter growled. "It wouldn't be the first time we had to reconsider our assumptions. The psychologists never would have gotten out of their rut if somebody hadn't gotten smart and realized that institutional reform sometimes requires turning the whole system on its head. That was quite a wall to climb."

"Yes, wasn't it," mused Parsons, scratching his bony jaw. "Only took them seventy years to climb it, thanks to a certain man's theories. I wonder how long it'll take military doctrine to crawl out of the pit you're digging for it?"

"We're not digging any pit," Porter exploded angrily. "We're exploring—nothing more. A phenomenon exists. We've known that, one way or another, for centuries. The fact that it doesn't seem to be bound by the same sort of traditional military logic we've observed elsewhere doesn't mean that it isn't governed by principles. But how can we define those principles? How can we define the limits of the phenomenon, for that matter? We can't work in the dark forever—we've got to have a working hypothesis to guide us."

"So you dreamed up this 'erosion' idea," said Parsons sourly.

"For a working hypothesis—yes. We've known for a long time that every junior officer has exceptional strategic potential to one degree or another. Not just a few here and there—every single one. It's a differentiating quality of effective military leadership. Just as the ability to think creatively in a crisis instead of falling back on doctrine is a differentiating quality."

"Fine," said Parsons. "Great. We can't prove that, of course, but I'll play along."

Porter glared at him. "When we began studying this strategic potential, we found out some curious things. For one thing, it seemed to be immensely more powerful and active in junior officers than in senior commanders. Somewhere along the line as an officer advances, something happens. We don't know what. We do know that the officer's strategic creativity gradually withdraws deeper and deeper into their decision-making process, burying itself farther and farther out of reach, just the way geological strata are buried deeper and deeper by accumulated sediment until the original formations are completely obscured." Porter paused, lighting his pipe. "That's why we have Crestwood—to try to discover why. What forces that potential underground? What buries it so deeply that senior officers can't access it anymore?"

"And you think you have an answer," said Parsons.

"We think we might be near an answer. We have a theory that explains the available data."

The transport vehicle stopped sharply as it left the main road. Anderson took the controls. In a few moments they were passing through the high gates of Crestwood, slowing down at the entrance to a long, low building.

"All right, young man—come along," said Porter. "I think we can show you our answer."

In the main administration building they donned the standard command filters required of all senior personnel at Crestwood. They were of a hard grey composite material, with a network of circuitry embedded in the substance, connected to a simple pocket-sized processor.

"The major problem," Porter said, "has been to shield the junior officers from any external command pressure, except those we wished to expose them to. Our goal is a perfectly controlled command environment. The filters are quite effective—a simple signal dampening system."

"It blocks off all types of command influence?" asked Parsons.

"As far as we can measure, yes."

"Which may not be very far."

Benjamin Anderson burst in: "What Colonel Porter is saying is that they seem effective for our purposes."

"But you don't know why," added Parsons.

"All right, we don't know why. Nobody knows why a dampening system works at the neurological level—why blame us?" They were walking down the main corridor and out through an open courtyard. Behind the buildings was a broad training field. A tactical exercise was in progress in one corner; across the field a group of obstacle courses, climbing walls, and other training equipment was in heavy use. The place was teeming with young officers, all engaged in intense activity. Occasionally a filtered supervisor hurried by; one waved to them as she corrected a lieutenant's form on the rappelling wall.

Anderson gestured toward the active training grounds. "This is what we do here, day in and day out. Officers on regular duty rotations, following structured schedules, participating in exercises and collaborative work. The therapeutic value of routine cannot be overstated—troubled officers often recover simply by immersing themselves in the normal activities."

They crossed into the next building, where strategy sessions were in progress. "Some of our officers are here only briefly," Porter explained as they walked along, "and some have been here for years. We maintain a top-ranking curriculum—your idea of a 'military academy' wasn't so far afield at that—with positions funded by Command Center resources. Other officers come to us—transfers, volunteers, officers from troubled units, officers of all ranks from second lieutenant on. Sometimes they stay until they have reached field grade, or go on to commands. As far as strategic doctrine research is concerned, we are not trying to be commanders. We are strictly observers. We try to place the officers in positions where they can develop what potential they have—without the presence of external command influences they would normally be subject to. The results have been remarkable."

He led them into a long, narrow room with chairs and monitors, facing a wide observation window. The room fell into semi-darkness, and through the window they could see three lieutenants, about two years out of the academy, working on a tactical problem in a large room.

"They're perfectly isolated from us," said Porter. "A variety of recording instruments are working. And before you ask, Dr. Parsons, they are all empirical instruments, and they would all defy any engineer's attempts to determine precisely what makes them work. We don't know exactly what makes them work, and we don't care—they work. That's all we need. Like that one, for instance—"

In the corner a flat screen was displaying a complex tactical map with shifting colored zones. It hung from the wall by two data cables which penetrated into the officers' room. There was no visible input device, nor an obvious control system. As the officers moved about and discussed strategy, the map shifted and evolved. Below it, a recording device clicked along in little spurts and starts of activity.

"What are they doing?" Parsons asked after watching the officers a few moments.

"Those three seem to work as a team, somehow. Each one, individually, had a fairly constant recordable strategic potential of about seventeen on the arbitrary scale we find useful here. Any two of them scale in at thirty-four to thirty-six. Put the three together and they operate somewhere in the neighborhood of six hundred on the same scale." Porter smiled. "This is an isolated phenomenon—it doesn't hold for any other three officers at Crestwood. Nor did we make any effort to place them together—they sought each other out naturally. One of our analysts spent two weeks trying to find out why the instruments weren't calibrated correctly. It wasn't the instruments, of course."

Porter nodded to an attendant, and peered around at Parsons. "Now, I want you to watch this very closely."

He opened a door and walked into the room with the officers. The tactical display continued to shift as the officers turned to Porter. He examined the strategic solution they were developing, and stopped to discuss it with them, his words audible through the observation room speakers. The officers engaged enthusiastically, apparently intrigued by the refinement he was proposing. He walked to the display and tapped a key sector with his finger.

The map quivered, and the display blazed with activity, but the solution held. Carefully Porter questioned all the foundational assumptions until the entire strategy hung on pure creative thinking, clearly unsupported by traditional doctrine. The officers watched it closely, and the assumptions shifted even further from convention....

Then, quite casually, Porter removed his command filter. The officers continued analyzing the strategy as the display gave three or four violent bursts of chaotic data and went dark.

The tactical solution collapsed entirely.

Moments later Porter was back in the observation room, leaving the officers busily reconstructing their approach. There was a little smile on his lips as he saw Parsons's face. "Perhaps you're beginning to see what I'm driving at," he said slowly.

"Yes," said Parsons. "I think I'm beginning to see." He scratched his jaw. "You think that it's senior command contact that drives the junior officer's potential underground—that somehow senior contact acts like a damper, a sort of colossal creativity-snuffer."

"That's what I think," said Porter.

"How do you know those officers didn't make you remove your filter?"

Porter blinked. "Why should they?"

"Maybe they wanted to see what would happen to their solution."

"But that wouldn't make any difference, would it? The solution still collapses."

Parsons paced down the narrow room. "This is very good," he said suddenly, his voice earnest. "You have fine facilities here, good personnel. And in spite of my flippancy, Colonel Porter, I have never imagined for a moment that you were not an acute observer and a careful, highly imaginative analyst. But suppose I told you, in perfect faith, that we have data that flatly contradicts everything you've told me today. Reproducible data, utterly incompatible with yours. What would you say to that?"

"I'd say you were wrong," said Porter. "You couldn't have such data. According to the things I am certain are true, what you're saying is sheer nonsense."

"And you'd express that opinion in a professional conference?"

"I would."

"And as an Authority on strategic doctrine," said Parsons slowly, "you would kill us then and there. You would strangle us professionally, discredit anything we did, cut us off cold." The tall man turned on him fiercely. "Are you blind, man? Can't you see what danger you're in? If you publish your monograph now, you will become an Authority in a field where the most devastating thing that could possibly happen would be—the appearance of an Authority."

Porter and Anderson rode back to the Queenstown Command Center in grim silence. At first Porter pretended to work; finally he snapped off the data reader in disgust and stared out the transport window. Parsons had gone on to the airfield to catch a flight back to Horizonville. It was a relief to see him go, Porter thought, and tried to force the thin, angry man firmly out of his mind. But somehow Parsons wouldn't leave.

"Stop worrying about it," Anderson urged. "He's a radical. He's crawled way out on a limb, and now he's afraid your theory is going to cut it off under him. Well, that's his worry, not yours." Anderson's face was intense. "Professionally, you're on unshakeable ground. Every great researcher has people like Parsons sniping at him. You just have to ignore them and keep going."

Porter shook his head. "Maybe. But this field of work is different from any other, Ben. It doesn't follow the rules. Maybe professional grounds aren't right at all, in this case."

Anderson snorted. "Surely there's nothing wrong with theorizing—"

"He wasn't objecting to the theory. He's afraid of what happens after the theory."

"So it seems. But why?"

"Have you ever considered what makes a man an Authority?"

"He knows more about his field than anybody else does."

"He seems to, you mean. And therefore, anything he says about it carries more weight than what anybody else says. Other researchers follow his lead. He develops ideas, formulates theories—and then defends them for all he's worth."

"But why shouldn't he?"

"Because a man can't fight for his life and reputation and still keep his objectivity," said Porter. "And what if he just happens to be wrong? Once he's an Authority the question of what's right and what's wrong gets lost in the shuffle. It's what he says that counts."

"But we know you're right," Anderson protested.

"Do we?"

"Of course we do! Look at our work! Look at what we've seen at Crestwood."

"Yes, I know." Porter's voice was weary. "But first I think we'd better check on Matthew Russell—"

An aide greeted them as they stepped off the elevator. "We called you at Crestwood, but you'd already left. The lieutenant—" She broke off helplessly. "He's in crisis, Colonel. He's worse than we ever imagined."

"What happened?"

"Nothing exactly—happened. I don't quite know how to describe it." She hurried them down the corridor and opened a door into the restricted evaluation room. "See what you think."

The lieutenant sat rigidly in the corner of the room. He looked up as they came in, but there was no flicker of recognition or relief on his pale face. The command filter was still in place. He just sat there, gripping a tactical manual tightly in his hands. The room was bare except for monitoring equipment—no training materials, no exercise apparatus, nothing that resembled the busy activity they had witnessed at Crestwood.

Porter crossed the room swiftly. "Matthew," he said.

The lieutenant didn't even look at him. He stared fixedly at the manual.

"Matthew!" Porter reached out for the book. The lieutenant drew back in alarm, clutching it to his chest. "Go away," he choked. "Go away, go away—" When Porter persisted the lieutenant jerked away violently.

Porter sat down at the table. "Matthew, listen to me." His voice was gentle. "I won't try to take it again. I promise."

"Go away."

"Do you know who I am?"

Russell's eyes shifted haltingly to Porter's face. He nodded. "Go away."

"Why are you afraid, Matthew?"

"I can't think. My head is clouded. I can't function. Go away."

"Why can't you think?"

"I—can't get it—off," the lieutenant said.

The filter, Porter thought suddenly. Something had suddenly gone horribly wrong—could the officer really be sensing the source of the trouble? Porter felt a cold knot gather in the pit of his stomach. He knew what happened when unfiltered senior command pressure struck a high-potential junior officer's mind. He had seen it a hundred times at Crestwood. But even more—he had felt it in his own experience, the weight of it. Like a violent physical constraint, the rigidity and fear and hierarchy and control buried and institutionalized in the senior command mind, crushing suddenly into the raw creativity of the junior officer's thinking like a smothering fog—it was a fearful thing. A healthy officer could survive it, even though the scar remained. But this officer was in crisis—

And yet an organism instinctively seeks its own healing. With trembling fingers Porter reached out and opened the release-catch on the filter. "Take it off, Matthew," he whispered.

The lieutenant blinked in amazement, and pulled the grey device from his head. Porter felt the familiar subtle shift in the room's atmosphere as the lieutenant stared at him. He could sense in his own awareness the cold chill of professional doubt radiating from the young officer. Then, suddenly, it began to fade. A sense of clarity—confidence and purpose and creative energy—swept in as the fear faded from the lieutenant's face.

The tactical manual fell to the floor.

They analyzed the data later, processing the evaluation files with greatest care, running them through the systems for the basic analysis and classification that all their data underwent. It was late that night when they had the report back in their hands.

Anderson stared at it angrily. "It's obviously wrong," he grated. "It doesn't fit. Stephen, it doesn't agree with anything we've observed before. There must be an error."

"Of course," said Porter. "According to the theory. The theory says that senior command contact is deadly to the developing junior officer. It smothers their potential through repeated contact until it atrophies completely. We've proved that, haven't we? Time after time. Everything goes according to the theory—except Matthew. But Matthew's strategic potential was atrophying in that restricted environment, until the distortion was threatening the balance of his professional capacity. Then he made a senior contact, and we saw how he recovered." Porter sank down to his desk wearily. "What are we going to do, Ben? Formulate a separate theory for Matthew?"

"Of course not," said Anderson. "The instruments were wrong. Somehow we misread the data—"

"Didn't you see his face?" Porter burst out. "Didn't you see how he responded? What do you want with an instrument reading?" He shook his head. "It's no good, Ben. Something different happened here, something we'd never counted on. It's something the theory just doesn't allow for."

They sat silently for a while. Then Anderson said: "What are you going to do?"

"I don't know," said Porter. "Maybe when we fell into this bramble bush we blinded ourselves with the urge to systematize—to line everything up in neat categories like pins in a display. Maybe we were so focused on systems thinking we missed the actual dynamics altogether."

"But the monograph is due! The Conference speech—"

"I think we'll make some changes in the monograph," Porter said slowly. "It'll be costly—but it might even be liberating. It's a pretty rigid, authoritarian presentation of ideas, as it stands. Very definitive and commanding. But a few revisions could change all that—" He rubbed his hands together thoughtfully. "How about it, Ben? Do we have nerve enough to be questioned? Do you think we could stand a little professional uncertainty, admitting we might be wrong? Because when I finish this monograph, we'll be challenged from every direction. There won't be any Authority in strategic doctrine for a while—and maybe that way one of the researchers who's really discovering the truth will get somebody to listen to him!

"Get your notepad! We've got work to do. And when we finish, I think we'll send a copy out Horizonville way. Might even persuade that young academic out there to come here and work with me—"
